claims.text: The initial material is a bulk equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy produced by conventional processing.
Composition-gradient thin-film deposition can systematically vary individual-element percentages across one substrate.
High-throughput mechanical characterization of a composition-gradient film can quantify composition-dependent mechanical-property changes.
Controlled deposition and room-temperature testing can ensure uniform film microstructure and minimize substrate effects.
Varying individual elemental percentages alters local lattice distortion.
Varying individual elemental percentages changes phase stability.
Increasing the relative Hf or Zr content increases atomic-size mismatch and lattice distortion.
Adjusting elemental percentages modifies the nature of atomic bonding.
Greater atomic-size mismatch impedes dislocation motion more effectively.
More effective impediment of dislocation motion increases strength and hardness.
Increasing Hf or Zr content may reduce ductility.
Film regions enriched in larger atoms will have greater hardness than the equiatomic baseline.
Film regions enriched in larger atoms will have greater tensile strength than the equiatomic baseline.
Film regions enriched in larger atoms will have lower ductility than the equiatomic baseline.
The mechanical properties of conventionally processed equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr are well documented.
Thin-film measurements may differ from bulk behavior because of scale effects and substrate interactions.
Room-temperature outcomes may not extend to high-temperature regimes.
Thin-film stress, measurement variability, and film-versus-bulk differences may affect the measured magnitude of the property changes.
